items.t: APEC summit: Trump seeks nuclear arms cuts, but few concrete results expected

The main issue on the table is nuclear disarmament, with Trump seeking to get the United States and China to reduce their stockpiles. items.t: Trump, Xi, Putin summit: What was it all about?
items.m: Donald Trump has left China after a historic first meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Ukraine was discussed without Kyiv or European leaders in the room, which raised eyebrows, though Trump defended dialogue with rivals and Putin said the talks created conditions for future agreements. Xi warned major powers against conflict, and topics included reducing nuclear risks, reforming the UN and increasing energy flows.

items.t: Damaged buildings and debris after Ukrainian attack on Russia's Kursk
items.m: At least 11 people were injured after a Ukrainian attack damaged residential buildings and public facilities in the southwestern Russian city of Kursk, according to regional Governor Alexander Khinshtein.

items.t: Weakened Putin is pinning his hopes on a Le Pen victory, Browder says
items.m: Kremlin critic Bill Browder tells Euronews that a weakened Vladimir Putin is using peace talks to buy time, hoping a far-right victory in France will fracture European support for Ukraine.

items.t: Ukraine peace deal 'not feasible' without Europe, Polish minister warns
items.m: Poland’s Deputy Foreign Minister Ignacy Niemczycki tells Euronews that Europe is indispensable to any Ukraine peace settlement, hinting that Kyiv’s allies are moving towards a military role in enforcing an agreement.

items.t: Dutch embassy in Kyiv damaged by a projectile crash nearby
items.m: A projectile struck the area behind the Dutch embassy in Ukraine on Thursday, causing minor damage to the building; no casualties were reported.

items.t: Putin hails ‘new chapter in the history of diplomacy’ after talks with Trump
items.m: Vladimir Putin says his meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping covered key global security issues, including the war in Ukraine, nuclear proliferation and freedom of navigation. The leaders also discussed maritime law, the role of the International Criminal Court and potential UN reforms.

items.t: NATO chief downplays Yalta 2.0 fears after Trump-Putin-Xi summit
items.m: Mark Rutte says meetings of major powers normal, praises Trump’s ‘Herculean efforts’ to achieve peace in Ukraine

items.t: Ukraine destroyed the Crimean Bridge. Putin has vowed to retaliate, but Russia has repeatedly failed to bring down bridges in Ukraine. Can Moscow deliver?
items.m: Ukraine’s attack on the Crimean Bridge showed that destroying structures like this with strikes launched from hundreds of kilometers away, in the face of active enemy air defense and electronic warfare, is possible. Before this, Russia had spent several months proving the opposite: every attempt to put the Dnipro bridges out of commission for any length of time had failed. But now Putin is once again threatening Ukraine with “far more painful” consequences in response from the Russian military.

items.t: A third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia’s Kerch Bridge to Crimea
items.m: Earlier strikes shut down the road section of the bridge that is a symbol of Moscow’s invasion.

items.t: Russia repels Ukrainian drones attack on oil facility in Tatarstan region, local authorities say
items.m: MOSCOW, Nov 19 - Russian air defence systems repelled a Ukrainian drone attack on oil facility in the Tatarstan region east of Moscow on Thursday, local authorities said, as Ukraine pounded Russian energy infrastructure during the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

items.t: Ukraine was main topic at Trump-Putin meeting, Kremlin says
items.m: MOSCOW, Nov 19 - The war in Ukraine dominated a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said on Thursday.

items.t: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
items.m: Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’ China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants. The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity. Continue reading...

items.m: The Russian leader invited European representatives to Moscow to discuss giving them a role in negotiations. It was unclear how serious the offer was.

items.t: Is Europe now in the shadow of a Trump, Putin and Xi alliance? – podcast
items.m: Andy Burnham is meeting western leaders in Berlin and Brussels this week, to discuss Ukraine and closer ties to the EU. Meanwhile, Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have met at the Apec summit in China. Is this the start of a global shift of power away from Europe, or was it just a hyped-up photo opportunity? You can read Pippa Crerar’s article on the EU’s approach to a reset with the UK here Continue reading...

items.t: Prince Harry says he is ready to rejoin British Army if needed amid Russia-Ukraine war
items.m: Prince Harry has said he would be willing to rejoin the British Army if the need arose, amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. The Duke of Sussex made the remarks during an unannounced visit to Ukraine, where he warned that Europe should be concerned about the growing threat from Russia. Harry served 10 years in the Army, completing two tours in Afghanistan as an Apache helicopter pilot.

Girls he coached had accused him of sexual harassment.

items.t: The Kremlin used to ask friendly outlets to play down its domestic policy chief, Sergey Kiriyenko. Journalists say they’re now told to mention him at every opportunity.
items.m: Sergey Kiriyenko, who heads domestic policy in Russia’s Presidential Administration, has generally kept a low profile in Russian politics. Since October, however, he has spoken regularly at public events about his favorite subject — the eventual return of Russian troops from the front in Ukraine and the need to “reintegrate” them into civilian life. Journalists at state-run and pro-government outlets have started following his appearances closely, even though the Kremlin used to ask them not to draw unnecessary attention to him. The comments came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz qualified the summit between the presidents of the United States, Russia and China as a "photo op". FRANCE 24's international affairs commentator Douglas Herbert explains.

items.t: As Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill turns 80, Meduza retraces how he went from backing Ukrainian self-determination to defending Moscow’s full-scale invasion
items.m: Patriarch Kirill (born Vladimir Gundyaev) turned 80 on November 20. Since 2009, he has led the Russian Orthodox Church while binding it ever more closely to the state. The Kremlin bolsters the church’s standing, and church leaders back the government’s agenda across the board. But Kirill wasn’t always such an open ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin and accomplice to his regime. Kirill’s own words show how the church became a political force and a vehicle for propaganda under his leadership. items.m: A Russian ballistic missile attack hit three bridges on Kyiv's Dnipro River and killed three people, the city's mayor said.

items.t: Three killed in missile strikes on Kyiv, mayor says, in biggest attack on bridges
items.m: KYIV, Nov 20 - A Russian ballistic missile attack hit three bridges on Kyiv's Dnipro River and killed three people, the city's mayor said on Friday, in the biggest strikes on routes connecting the left and right banks of Ukraine's capital since the start of the war.

items.t: Russia wants people in bankruptcy to sign up to fight in Ukraine. Under a new bill, recruits could keep their property and creditors would take the loss.
items.m: The Russian government has submitted a bill to the State Duma that would let new recruits who sign military contracts and go to fight against Ukraine keep assets worth up to 10 million rubles in total during bankruptcy.

items.t: Polish army investigates report of unknown objects near Ukraine border
